title: Food poisoning and botulism
summary: Diarrhea, stomach pain or cramps, nausea, vomiting and fever are the usual signs of food poisoning; care is in the Severe vomiting or diarrhea and Dehydration protocols. Double vision, blurred vision, drooping eyelids, slurred speech, trouble swallowing or breathing, or muscle weakness can be botulism, a medical emergency: see a doctor or go to an emergency room now. Never give honey to a baby under 1 year.
doFirst: Vomiting or diarrhea after eating: use the Severe vomiting or diarrhea and Dehydration protocols.

Double vision, blurred vision, drooping eyelids, slurred speech, trouble swallowing, trouble breathing, trouble moving the eyes or muscle weakness? It can be botulism. Botulism is a medical emergency: see a doctor or go to the emergency room now. Do not wait (CDC).

A baby who is sluggish and “floppy”, constipated, feeds poorly, has drooping eyelids, pupils slow to react to light, a weak cry or less expression than usual can have botulism too (CDC, New York State Department of Health). Get them to a doctor now.

Throw away food that might be contaminated, and never taste it (CDC). A suspect can or jar that is still sealed: bag it unopened. Leaking or open: make it harmless first, as in Getting rid of a suspect can or jar (National Center for Home Food Preservation).
Never give honey to a baby under 1 year (New York State Department of Health).

blocks.p: The most common signs are diarrhea, stomach pain or cramps, nausea, vomiting and fever (CDC). Some germs make you sick within a few hours of eating; others take a few days (CDC).

If you have diarrhea or vomiting, drink plenty of fluids so you don’t get dehydrated (CDC). How to care for someone, what to give them to drink, and the danger signs that mean they need medical help are in the protocols.
Pregnant and have a fever and other flu-like symptoms? See a doctor (CDC).

Two or more people sick from the same food or drink is an outbreak (CDC). Check the shared food and water, keep anyone who was sick away from food and the group’s water, and keep hands clean: Stomach illness in a group says how, and for how long.
Several people sick at once can also be carbon monoxide from a stove, heater or engine, or a shared poison: the Severe vomiting or diarrhea protocol checks for these.
Botulism is caused by a toxin that attacks the body’s nerves and causes muscle weakness. It can weaken the muscles used in breathing, which can lead to difficulty breathing and even death (CDC).

blocks.warn: Botulism is a medical emergency. If you or your child has signs of botulism, see your doctor or go to the emergency room immediately. Do not wait (CDC).

list: From food, also vomiting, nausea, stomach pain and diarrhea

blocks.p: New York State Department of Health adds a dry mouth. Someone with botulism might not have all of these at the same time (CDC).

Babies with botulism might have constipation, poor feeding, drooping eyelids, pupils that are slow to react to light, a face showing less expression than usual, and a weak cry that sounds different than usual (CDC). They typically seem sluggish and “floppy” (New York State Department of Health).

When it starts: from food, signs typically appear 12 to 72 hours after eating, but can start anywhere from 2 hours to 8 days after (New York State Department of Health). For a baby it can be up to 30 days (New York State Department of Health).

Botulism needs a hospital. Caught early, it can be treated with a drug called antitoxin, which stops the toxin doing more harm; if it is severe, the person may need a breathing machine (New York State Department of Health). It does not spread from person to person (New York State Department of Health).

If no doctor or hospital can be reached: no source opened for this app gives steps for botulism without one. This app’s reading: keep trying to reach medical care, and if the person stops responding and is not breathing normally, use the CPR protocols.

blocks.warn: Honey is a known source of botulism in babies. Never feed honey to a baby under 1 year of age (New York State Department of Health).

sections.h: Getting rid of a suspect can or jar

blocks.p: Signs that a can or jar may be contaminated are in Is it still good? Treat any suspect container of low-acid food, tomatoes included, as if it has botulism toxin in it (National Center for Home Food Preservation).

blocks.warn: Botulism toxin can kill if it is swallowed or gets in through any opening in the skin. Keep suspect food and liquid off your skin, and wear rubber or heavy plastic gloves to handle it (National Center for Home Food Preservation). Never taste it (CDC).

list: Still sealed: put the can or jar in a heavy garbage bag, close the bag, and put it in a regular trash container (National Center for Home Food Preservation).
Unsealed, open or leaking: it must be made harmless before it goes in the trash (National Center for Home Food Preservation). The steps are below.

steps: Put on disposable rubber or heavy plastic gloves (National Center for Home Food Preservation).
Lay the suspect cans or jars and their lids on their sides in a stockpot of 8 quarts (7.6 L) or larger (National Center for Home Food Preservation).
Wash your gloved hands well (National Center for Home Food Preservation).
Add water carefully, without splashing, until it covers the containers by at least 1 inch (2.5 cm) (National Center for Home Food Preservation).
Put a lid on the pot, bring the water to a boil, and boil for 30 minutes (National Center for Home Food Preservation).
Let it cool, then put the containers, lids and food in the trash (National Center for Home Food Preservation).
Throw away the gloves when you are done (National Center for Home Food Preservation).

blocks.p: A spill from a suspect can or jar, and anything it touched (work surfaces, equipment, can openers, clothing): the National Center for Home Food Preservation’s clean-up, in its own words and order:

blocks.warn: This app’s own caution: this bleach mix is for this clean-up only. Never use it for drinking water, and never as an everyday sanitizer for dishes or food surfaces: for those, use Clean and disinfect. Never mix bleach with ammonia or any other cleaner (CDC; Clean and disinfect).

steps: Wear rubber or heavy plastic gloves (National Center for Home Food Preservation).
Make a fresh solution of 1 part unscented liquid household chlorine bleach (5 to 6% sodium hypochlorite) to 5 parts clean water (National Center for Home Food Preservation).
Spray or wet the contaminated surfaces with the bleach solution and let it stand for 30 minutes (National Center for Home Food Preservation).
Wearing gloves, wipe up the treated spill with paper towels, taking care not to spread the contamination (National Center for Home Food Preservation).
Put the paper towels in a plastic bag before they go in the trash (National Center for Home Food Preservation).
Put the bleach solution on all the surfaces and equipment again, let it stand for 30 minutes, and rinse (National Center for Home Food Preservation).
Last, wash everything you cleaned thoroughly: counters, containers, equipment, clothing (National Center for Home Food Preservation).
Throw away the gloves when the clean-up is done (National Center for Home Food Preservation).

blocks.p: Bleach is an irritant itself: don’t breathe it in or let it touch your skin (National Center for Home Food Preservation).

Other jars or cans from the same batch: no source opened for this app says what to do with them. This app’s own caution: if one container from a batch shows any sign in Is it still good?, or someone got sick after eating from it, treat the whole batch as suspect and get rid of it the same way.
